title: Reduced and identity-component factors of a finite commutative group over a perfect field
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of characteristic $p>0$ such that every element of $k$ is a $p$-th power. Let $G$ be a commutative finite $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Let $G^\circ$ be the connected component containing its identity, endowed with its open-and-closed subscheme structure (connectedness is [def-weil-connected-scheme]), and let $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ be the reduced closed subscheme [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction]: in an affine presentation $G=\operatorname{Spec}B$ it is $\operatorname{Spec}(B/\sqrt{(0)})$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Both $G^\circ$ and $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]; $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is finite etale over $k$ [def-weil-etale-morphism]. Multiplication induces an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes $$G^\circ\times_k G_{\mathrm{red}}\xrightarrow{\sim}G.$$ The factor $G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is not required to be a constant group scheme over $k$.

source.place: Proposition 11.3 and its proof, printed p.210; the semidirect product there is a direct product for a commutative G. Identity components with open-and-closed structure: Proposition 2.37, printed pp.51-52.

proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ finite-dimensional over $k$. Put $C=B/\sqrt{(0)}$ and $R=G_{\mathrm{red}}=\operatorname{Spec}C$. The reduced-induced-subscheme theorem ensures that $C$ is reduced. It is finite-dimensional, being a quotient of $B$; hence the finite-reduced-perfect-algebra lemma and the affine ring-map criterion make $R$ finite etale. The tensor lemma makes $C\otimes_kC$ reduced. Any map from $B$ to a reduced ring kills every nilpotent. Apply this to the restrictions of multiplication $R\times_kR\to G$, inversion $R\to G$, and the identity $\operatorname{Spec}k\to G$: each factors uniquely through $R\hookrightarrow G$. The group axioms follow after composing with this closed immersion, since on affine rings its quotient map is surjective. Thus $R$ is a closed subgroup scheme; no assertion about its being constant is used.

source.place: Proposition 11.3, first use of Corollary 1.39; Proposition 1.38 and its proof, printed pp.18 and 210. Algebraic inputs also Stacks 00I4 and 00U3.

proof.text: Apply the component-scheme theorem to $G$, writing $P=\Pi_k(G)$ and $q=q_G$. Here $G$ is affine by finiteness and separated because the diagonal of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ is induced by the surjective multiplication map $B\otimes_kB\to B$. The functor $\Pi_k$ preserves products and the terminal scheme, so applying it to multiplication, inverse, identity and each group-axiom diagram gives a commutative group scheme structure on $P$, with $q$ a homomorphism. The identity $e_P$ is an open-and-closed copy of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ in $P$: its finite etale coordinate algebra is a product of finite separable fields, and a $k$-algebra map from such a product to $k$ selects a factor equal to $k$. Consequently $H=G\times_{P,e_P}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is an open-and-closed subgroup scheme. Indeed its $T$-points are the kernel of $q:G(T)\to P(T)$ for every $k$-scheme $T$. The component-scheme theorem says that its underlying space is the connected component of the identity. The pullback of this open immersion equips it with the open subscheme structure, so $H$ is exactly the $G^\circ$ of the item, including its possibly nonreduced structure.

source.place: Proposition 2.37(b,d), printed pp.51-52, deduced by applying Propositions 1.29-1.31 to the group diagrams; Proposition 1.34, pp.16-17.

proof.text: Let $K$ be a separable closure of $k$. It is perfect: let $a\in K$. Since $K/k$ is separable, $a$ is separable over $k$ and hence over $k(a^p)$, while it is a root of $X^p-a^p=(X-a)^p$ over $k(a^p)$; so $a\in k(a^p)=k[a^p]$. Writing $a=\sum_i c_ia^{pi}$ with $c_i\in k$ and $c_i=d_i^p$, $d_i\in k$, gives $a=(\sum_i d_ia^i)^p$ with $\sum_i d_ia^i\in K$. It is algebraically closed: an irreducible polynomial over $K$ with zero derivative is, by perfectness, a $p$-th power and cannot be irreducible; otherwise it is separable and has degree one by separable closedness. The component theorem identifies $q_K$ with the component map of $G_K$. The underlying space of the finite $K$-scheme $G_K$ is finite discrete by the zero-dimensional finite-type lemma: every prime quotient of its finite-dimensional coordinate algebra is a finite-dimensional domain over $K$, hence a field (multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective, hence surjective, linear endomorphism). Its components are therefore single points. Each residue field is a finite extension of the algebraically closed field $K$, hence $K$. Thus $q_K$ gives a bijection $G(K)\to P(K)$. Every map $B\to K$ kills $\sqrt{(0)}$, giving $R(K)=G(K)$. It follows that $u=q|_R:R\to P$ is bijective on $K$-points. Both its source and target are etale. By full faithfulness of the etale geometric-point functor, the inverse of this equivariant bijection lifts to a $k$-morphism $v:P\to R$, and faithfulness gives $uv=1$ and $vu=1$. As $u$ is a homomorphism, its inverse is a homomorphism too.

source.place: Proposition 11.3, geometric-point comparison, printed p.210; finite discreteness is Proposition 11.2, pp.209-210. Etale full faithfulness is also Stacks 03QR.

proof.text: Put $r=v\circ q:G\to R$ and let $j:R\hookrightarrow G$ be the inclusion. The morphism $a:G\to G$, $a(x)=xj(r(x))^{-1}$, satisfies $q(a(x))=q(x)u(r(x))^{-1}=e_P$. The kernel fibre product therefore gives a morphism $a:G\to H$. Multiplication $m:H\times_kR\to G$ and $(a,r):G\to H\times_kR$ are inverse morphisms: $m(a(x),r(x))=x$, while for $h\in H(T)$ and $z\in R(T)$ one has $r(hj(z))=z$ and $a(hj(z))=h$. These identities are functorial for every test scheme $T$, so they are identities of scheme morphisms. Finally commutativity gives $(h_1j(z_1))(h_2j(z_2))=(h_1h_2)j(z_1z_2)$ on every $T$, proving $m$ is a homomorphism. Its inverse is then a homomorphism. With $H=G^\circ$ and $R=G_{\mathrm{red}}$ this is the asserted isomorphism of group schemes.
